summary: CCC stone fire tower on Fort Mountain, Murray County: completed 1935 (not 1938), burned 1971, restored 2014-15, NHLR-registered 2012.

facts.design: 50-foot CCC stone tower; the original wood and glass top burned in 1971 and was rebuilt in the restoration

access.note: Inside Fort Mountain State Park and reached on foot by park trails. A 2018 Register visit report says park staff give guided tours of the tower. No current hours or tour times were found.

visit.trail_note: Reached by a one-mile loop: up the West Overlook Trail and back by the CCC Stone Tower Trail. The park page lists the tower with a weather-permitting note.

events.note: Completed by the CCC; the state report and engineering article say 1935. The Register says 1938 and Forest Lookouts says 1936.
Top burned. The Register attributes the fire to vandals; the state and engineering sources give no cause.
Stone tower fell into disuse after the fire, per the state report
Registered May 25, 2012 as US 943, GA 13; nominated by park manager Brian Ensley
Restoration 2014-15 per the state report; completed in fall 2015 per the engineering article. Cupola rebuilt.

corrections.why: The state restoration report and the engineering article both say the tower was completed in 1935. The Register's 1938 is contradicted by both.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Register says 1938, Forest Lookouts says 1936, and the state report and engineering article say completed 1935. The story and the proposed correction follow the 1935 date.
The Register blames vandals for the early 1970s fire. The state and engineering sources do not name a cause, so the story reports only what each source says.
The Register dates the restoration to around 2018, but a photo on that page is captioned April 2016 after restoration. The state report and engineering article date the work to 2014-2015.
The state report says about $189,000 was allocated in 2014. The engineering article gives a $225,000 project. These may be an allocation and a final cost, but the sources do not say so.

notes_for_editor: Seven sources. The conflicts are the build year (1935, 1936 or 1938), the cause of the 1971 fire, the restoration date, and the cost. Staffing: the 2018 Register visit report answers yes to a staffing question, but its meaning is not stated; the fire watch ended in the early 1960s per the state report. Access is marked public because of the park trail and guided-tour evidence; current hours were not verified. The brief's height of 15.2 m matches 50 ft in the Register and Forest Lookouts.
